senses.gloss: Not straight; at an angle.
examples: The picture on the wall was hanging *askew*.
His glasses sat *askew* after the fall.
She came in with her hat knocked *askew* by the wind.

contrast: In *The baby is asleep* it works like an adjective, but it never goes before a noun: *a sleeping baby*, not *an asleep baby*.

senses.gloss: Into or in a state of sleep.
examples: I fell *asleep* on the couch watching TV.
The kids were fast *asleep* by nine.
Try not to fall *asleep* at the wheel.

senses.gloss: Of an arm or leg: numb from pressure.
examples: My foot fell *asleep* during the long meeting.
My leg's fallen *asleep* — give me a second.

senses.gloss: In a confident, forceful way that makes others listen.
examples: She learned to speak *assertively* in meetings.
If the landlord ignores you, follow up *assertively* in writing.
He *assertively* pushed for a raise.

senses.gloss: With great care and steady effort.
examples: She *assiduously* avoided talking about her past.
The staff worked *assiduously* to keep the records accurate.
He had *assiduously* built a reputation for honesty.

senses.gloss: Certainly; without doubt.
examples: This is *assuredly* not the last we'll hear of it.
"Will you be there?" "Most *assuredly*."
The new rules will *assuredly* face a legal challenge.

type: stance — a comment on the sentence; also degree
position: front — as a comment; before an adjective or adverb as a degree word

senses.gloss: In a way that causes great surprise; to a surprising degree.
examples: *Astonishingly*, no one was hurt in the crash.
The results were *astonishingly* good.
She learned the language *astonishingly* fast.

position: before its word — *astronomically high*; also end
modifies: adjectives, and verbs of rising and costing

senses.gloss: To an extremely high degree, especially of prices or numbers.
examples: Rents in the city have risen *astronomically*.
The odds against it are *astronomically* high.
Tuition has gone up *astronomically* since the 1980s.

senses.gloss: In a sharp, clever way that shows good judgment.
examples: She *astutely* noticed the error in the contract.
As one critic *astutely* pointed out, the plan had no budget.
He invested *astutely* and retired early.

senses.gloss: In a way that is not the same on both sides.
examples: The building was designed *asymmetrically*, with one tall tower.
Her hair was cut *asymmetrically*, longer on the left.
The weight was distributed *asymmetrically*, so the shelf tipped over.

position: end — also before its word as a degree word

senses.gloss: Very badly; in a shockingly bad or cruel way.
examples: The team played *atrociously* in the second half.
The prisoners were treated *atrociously*.
The service at that restaurant is *atrociously* slow.

senses.gloss: With close attention.
examples: The students listened *attentively* to the speaker.
She watched *attentively* as the chef sliced the fish.
The nurses cared for him *attentively* day and night.

position: end — also before a past participle: *attractively priced*

senses.gloss: In a way that is pleasing to look at or appealing.
examples: The dishes were *attractively* arranged on the table.
The house is *attractively* priced for the neighborhood.
She dressed *attractively* but simply.

position: before its word — mostly an adjective; also front, as a comment

senses.gloss: In a way that is not typical or usual.
examples: It was *atypically* warm for February.
*Atypically*, the boss arrived late and said nothing.
The patient responded *atypically* to the drug.

senses.gloss: In a bold, daring way that ignores risk or convention.
examples: The thieves *audaciously* robbed the bank in broad daylight.
She *audaciously* asked the CEO for his job.
The museum was *audaciously* designed, with no straight walls.

senses.gloss: Loudly enough to be heard.
examples: He sighed *audibly* when the meeting ran late.
Please speak *audibly* so the back row can hear you.
The audience gasped *audibly*.

senses.gloss: In a way that suggests future success.
examples: The season began *auspiciously* with three straight wins.
Their partnership started *auspiciously*.
The trip didn't begin *auspiciously* — we missed our flight.

position: before its word — mostly a past participle: *austerely furnished*; also end

senses.gloss: In a plain, strict way, with no comfort or decoration.
examples: The monks' rooms were *austerely* furnished.
She lived *austerely* on a small pension.
The chapel was *austerely* beautiful, with bare stone walls.

position: end — also mid, and before an adjective

senses.gloss: In a real, genuine, or true-to-the-original way.
examples: The restaurant serves *authentically* Mexican food.
It's hard to act *authentically* on camera.
The film *authentically* recreates 1960s Detroit.

senses.gloss: With confidence and expert knowledge, in a way people trust.
examples: She spoke *authoritatively* about climate policy.
No one can say *authoritatively* what caused the fire.
He answered *authoritatively*, as if he'd been there.

senses.gloss: With total power, ignoring what others think.
examples: The founder ran the company *autocratically* for decades.
He governed *autocratically* and jailed his critics.
Don't make decisions *autocratically* — ask the team.

senses.gloss: By itself, without a person controlling it; or as a fixed result of something.
examples: The doors open *automatically* when you walk up to them.
If you pay late, a fee is added *automatically*.
The app saves your work *automatically* every five minutes.

senses.gloss: Without thinking about it.
examples: I *automatically* reached for my phone when I woke up.
She said thank you *automatically*, without looking up.

senses.gloss: With great eagerness and interest.
examples: She *avidly* reads every mystery novel she can find.
He followed the election results *avidly*.
As a kid, I *avidly* collected baseball cards.

form: flat — the same form as the adjective *awful*
contrast: Informal spoken American; careful writing uses *awfully* (*awfully cold*). In *an awful lot*, *awful* is an adjective describing *lot*.

senses.gloss: Very; extremely.
examples: It's *awful* cold out there this morning.
That's an *awful* big dog for such a small apartment.
She seemed *awful* tired when she got home.

contrast: Write *awhile* as one word only with no preposition before it (*stay awhile*). After *for* or *in*, write two words: *for a while*, *in a while*.

senses.gloss: For a short time.
examples: Why don't you stay *awhile* and have some coffee?
Let's sit here *awhile* and rest.
The kids played outside *awhile* before dinner.

senses.gloss: In a clumsy way, without ease or grace.
examples: He danced *awkwardly* at the wedding.
She fell *awkwardly* and twisted her ankle.

senses.gloss: In an embarrassing or uncomfortable way.
examples: They stood *awkwardly* in silence after the argument.
The meeting ended *awkwardly* when no one knew what to say.
He laughed *awkwardly* at the boss's joke.

senses.gloss: Away from what was planned or expected; wrong.
examples: Something went *awry* during the launch.
Their plans for the weekend went badly *awry*.

senses.gloss: Out of the normal or correct position; crooked.
examples: His tie was *awry* after the long day.
The wind had blown her hair *awry*.

senses.gloss: In or into the area behind a theater stage.
examples: We went *backstage* to meet the band after the show.
The actors were waiting nervously *backstage*.
Reporters aren't allowed *backstage* during the ceremony.

contrast: American English uses both *backward* and *backwards* as adverbs, and careful writing leans to *backward*; British English prefers *backwards*. Only *backward* is an adjective: *a backward glance*.

senses.gloss: Toward the back; in the direction behind you.
examples: She took a step *backwards* and tripped over the cat.
He fell *backwards* into the pool.
The car started rolling *backwards* down the hill.

senses.gloss: In reverse order, or with the back part in front.
examples: Can you say the alphabet *backwards*?
You've got your sweater on *backwards*.
Count *backwards* from ten.

form: flat — the same form as the adjective *bad*
contrast: Informal spoken American; careful writing uses *badly* (*badly hurt*). After linking verbs *bad* is an adjective and correct in any style: *I feel bad*, not *I feel badly*.

senses.gloss: Very much; seriously.
examples: I need a vacation so *bad*.
He got hurt pretty *bad* in the crash.
Nobody wanted that job *worse* than she did.

senses.gloss: In a plain, direct way, with nothing to soften it.
examples: "You're fired," he said *baldly*.
To put it *baldly*, we're out of money.
The report *baldly* states that the bridge is unsafe.

form: flat — the same form as the adjective *bareback*

senses.gloss: On a horse without a saddle.
examples: She learned to ride *bareback* on her grandfather's farm.
The kids rode the pony *bareback* around the field.
Riding *bareback* takes good balance.

form: flat — the same form as the adjective *barefoot*; *barefooted* also exists

senses.gloss: Without shoes or socks.
examples: The children ran *barefoot* along the beach.
Don't walk around *barefoot* — there's broken glass.
He came to the door *barefoot* and half asleep.

senses.gloss: In a shy, easily embarrassed way.
examples: She smiled *bashfully* when he complimented her.
The boy looked down *bashfully* at his shoes.
He *bashfully* admitted he had written the poem.

position: after its word — after the year or century
contrast: *B.C.* goes after the year (*44 B.C.*), but *A.D.* traditionally goes before it (*A.D. 79*). Scholarly and neutral writing often uses *B.C.E.* and *C.E.* instead.

senses.gloss: Before the traditional date of the birth of Christ, used after a year.
examples: Julius Caesar was killed in 44 *B.C.*
The temple was built around 500 *B.C.*
The city was founded in the eighth century *B.C.*

position: after its word — after the year or century
form: abbreviation of *before the Common Era*; also written *BCE*

senses.gloss: Before the Common Era; the same years as *B.C.*, used after a year.
examples: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 *B.C.E.*
Confucius was born in 551 *B.C.E.*
The clay tablets date from the third millennium *B.C.E.*

position: end — also before a past participle: *beautifully restored*

senses.gloss: In a beautiful way; very well.
examples: She sings *beautifully*.
The old house has been *beautifully* restored.
The new plan worked *beautifully*.

senses.gloss: Later than it should have happened.
examples: The company *belatedly* apologized for the data leak.
He *belatedly* realized he'd left his wallet at home.
I wished her a happy birthday *belatedly*, two days after.

senses.gloss: In a way that can be believed; convincingly.
examples: The actor plays a doctor very *believably*.
The characters are *believably* drawn.
She lied *believably* enough to fool the police.

senses.gloss: In an angry, aggressive way, ready to fight.
examples: He *belligerently* refused to show his ID.
The drunk customer shouted *belligerently* at the staff.
She stared *belligerently* at anyone who questioned her.

senses.gloss: In a kind, well-meaning way, often from a position of power.
examples: The old man smiled *benevolently* at the children.
By most accounts, the king ruled *benevolently*.
She looked on *benevolently* as the students celebrated.

senses.gloss: In a kind, gentle, harmless way.
examples: The professor smiled *benignly* at the nervous student.
The dog looked up *benignly* from its bed.
The policy was *benignly* intended but caused real harm.

contrast: Usually a preposition with an object (*between the two houses*). It is an adverb when the object is left out: *two houses with a garden in between*.

senses.gloss: In the space or time that separates two things.
examples: There's a hotel at each end of the street and shops *in between*.
The two storms hit a week apart, with sunny days *in between*.
Good restaurants are few and far *between* in this town.

position: before its word — mostly an adjective

senses.gloss: To a degree that confuses you.
examples: The tax rules are *bewilderingly* complex.
The menu offered a *bewilderingly* long list of options.
Prices changed *bewilderingly* fast that year.

contrast: Usually a preposition (*beyond the river*, *beyond belief*). It is an adverb when nothing follows it: *the hills beyond*, *2030 and beyond*.

senses.gloss: Farther away; on the far side.
examples: From the porch you can see the lake and the mountains *beyond*.
The road ends at the gate, and there's only desert *beyond*.

senses.gloss: Later in time or further in amount; after that.
examples: The plan covers the next five years and *beyond*.
Kids in third grade and *beyond* can join the club.

contrast: *Biannually* means twice a year; *biennially* means every two years. Readers often confuse them, so when it matters, write *twice a year* or *every two years*.

senses.gloss: Twice a year.
examples: The committee meets *biannually*, in March and September.
The newsletter is published *biannually*.
Prices are reviewed *biannually*.

contrast: *Biennially* means every two years; *biannually* means twice a year. When it matters, write *every two years* or *twice a year*.

senses.gloss: Once every two years.
examples: The art festival is held *biennially*.
The license must be renewed *biennially*.
Elections for the board take place *biennially*.

form: flat — the same form as the adjective *big*
contrast: Informal and limited to a few verbs. In *a big win* or *a big dream*, *big* is an adjective.

senses.gloss: On a large scale; ambitiously or with great success.
examples: If you want to grow the business, you have to think *big*.
She won *big* at the poker table last night.
Next year, we're going to dream even *bigger*.

senses.gloss: In a boastful way.
examples: He talks *big*, but he never follows through.
Don't talk *big* if you can't back it up.

senses.gloss: Between two sides, especially two countries.
examples: The two countries agreed to settle the dispute *bilaterally*.
Trade issues are often handled *bilaterally* rather than through the UN.
The deal was negotiated *bilaterally*, without the rest of the alliance.

senses.gloss: In two languages.
examples: Their kids are being raised *bilingually*, in English and Russian.
The school teaches math and science *bilingually*.
All the signs at the airport are printed *bilingually*.

ru: раз в два месяца; дважды в месяц
contrast: Ambiguous: it usually means every two months but sometimes twice a month. If the difference matters, write *every other month* or *twice a month*. Also an adjective: *a bimonthly magazine*.

senses.gloss: Every two months, or sometimes twice a month.
senses.ru: раз в два месяца; дважды в месяц
examples: The magazine is published *bimonthly*.
The club meets *bimonthly*, in odd-numbered months.
We pay the water bill *bimonthly*.

position: end — also before its word: *bitingly cold*

senses.gloss: In a sharp, sarcastic way meant to hurt.
examples: She commented *bitingly* on his lack of experience.
The review was *bitingly* funny.

senses.gloss: Extremely, of cold or wind.
examples: It was *bitingly* cold on the ski lift.
A *bitingly* cold wind blew off the river.

form: flat — the same form as the adjective *bitter*
contrast: Only in *bitter cold*. Elsewhere *bitter* is an adjective: *bitter coffee*, *a bitter fight*.

senses.gloss: Extremely, of cold weather.
examples: It was *bitter* cold on the morning of the parade.
The wind off the lake gets *bitter* cold in January.
Chicago can stay *bitter* cold for weeks at a time.

contrast: In American usage it almost always means every two weeks (*paid biweekly*), but it can also mean twice a week; *every other week* is unambiguous. Also an adjective: *a biweekly paycheck*.

senses.gloss: Every two weeks.
examples: Most employees here are paid *biweekly*.
The team meets *biweekly* on Tuesdays.
The newsletter goes out *biweekly*.

senses.gloss: In a calm, mild way that shows no strong feeling or interest.
examples: "That's not my problem," the clerk said *blandly*.
He smiled *blandly* and changed the subject.
The press release *blandly* described the layoffs as a restructuring.

senses.gloss: With no expression, often because you do not understand.
examples: She stared *blankly* at the math problem.
He looked at me *blankly* when I mentioned the meeting.
The students gazed *blankly* at the board.

position: before its word — *blatantly false*; also mid

senses.gloss: In an obvious and shameless way.
examples: The ad was *blatantly* misleading.
He *blatantly* ignored the stop sign.
That's a *blatantly* false statement.

senses.gloss: In a cold, gloomy, or hopeless way.
examples: "We'll never get out of here," he said *bleakly*.
She stared *bleakly* out at the rain.
The report *bleakly* predicts more job losses.

type: degree — with a sense of relief; also stance
position: before its word — *blessedly quiet*; also front

senses.gloss: In a welcome way that brings relief.
examples: The house was *blessedly* quiet after the kids left.
*Blessedly*, the rain stopped before the ceremony.
The drive home was *blessedly* short.

senses.gloss: Without being able to see.
examples: He felt around *blindly* for the light switch.
She ran *blindly* through the smoke.

senses.gloss: Without thinking or asking questions.
examples: Don't *blindly* trust everything you read online.
The soldiers followed orders *blindly*.
He *blindly* accepted the first offer.

position: before its word — *blissfully happy*, *blissfully unaware*; also end

senses.gloss: In a completely happy or untroubled way.
examples: They were *blissfully* unaware of the storm coming their way.
The baby slept *blissfully* through the noise.
The newlyweds seemed *blissfully* happy.

senses.gloss: In a casual, careless way, without noticing or caring about problems.
examples: He *blithely* ignored the warning signs.
She *blithely* assumed someone else would pay.
The company *blithely* promised results it couldn't deliver.

type: manner; also viewpoint in *to put it bluntly*
position: end — also front in *to put it bluntly*

senses.gloss: In a direct, honest way, without trying to be polite.
examples: She told him *bluntly* that his work wasn't good enough.
To put it *bluntly*, we can't afford it.
The doctor spoke *bluntly* about the risks.

senses.gloss: In a way that shows too much pride in yourself.
examples: He talked *boastfully* about his new car.
"I've never lost a match," she said *boastfully*.
The ad *boastfully* claimed to be the best in town.

position: end — after verbs of lifting and moving
contrast: More often an adjective: *bodily harm*, *bodily fluids*.

senses.gloss: By taking hold of the whole body; by physical force.
examples: The bouncer picked him up *bodily* and carried him out.
She was lifted *bodily* from the wreck.
The two protesters were removed *bodily* from the meeting.

form: the -ing form of *boil*, used as a degree word

senses.gloss: Extremely; used only in *boiling hot*.
examples: The coffee was *boiling* hot.
It gets *boiling* hot in the attic by noon.
Don't touch the pan — it's still *boiling* hot.

senses.gloss: In a loud, energetic, and cheerful way.
examples: The fans cheered *boisterously* after the goal.
The kids played *boisterously* in the backyard.
They laughed *boisterously* at the next table.

senses.gloss: In a brave, confident way that takes risks.
examples: She *boldly* asked for a promotion in her first month.
The company moved *boldly* into new markets.
The walls were *boldly* painted in red and orange.

contrast: Only in *bolt upright*. Elsewhere *bolt* is a noun (*a bolt of lightning*) or a verb (*The horse bolted*).

senses.gloss: Completely straight; used only in *bolt upright*.
examples: She sat *bolt* upright in bed when the phone rang.
He stood *bolt* upright as the general walked in.
The crash made everyone sit *bolt* upright.

senses.gloss: In a rude, crude way, with no regard for other people.
examples: He behaved *boorishly* at the dinner party.
A few fans acted *boorishly*, yelling insults at the players' families.
She was tired of tourists who *boorishly* ignored the museum rules.

position: before its word — *boringly predictable*; also end

senses.gloss: In a dull, uninteresting way.
examples: The movie was *boringly* predictable.
He spoke *boringly* for an hour about tax law.
The plan is *boringly* simple, and that's why it works.

position: end — also before an adjective: *boyishly handsome*

senses.gloss: In a way typical of a boy; young and charming.
examples: He grinned *boyishly* when she laughed.
At fifty, he was still *boyishly* handsome.
The senator *boyishly* ran a hand through his hair.

senses.gloss: In a loud, overconfident way.
examples: The young CEO *brashly* predicted he'd beat Amazon.
He spoke *brashly* about winning the title.
She *brashly* ignored the advice of more experienced colleagues.

senses.gloss: In a way that shows courage.
examples: The firefighters *bravely* entered the burning building.
She fought the illness *bravely* for years.
He smiled *bravely*, though he was clearly in pain.

senses.gloss: In an open, shameless way, without embarrassment.
examples: The thief *brazenly* walked out with a TV in broad daylight.
He *brazenly* lied to the judge.
Some drivers *brazenly* run red lights.

senses.gloss: While out of breath.
examples: She ran up the stairs and arrived *breathlessly* at the door.
"I made it," he said *breathlessly*.

senses.gloss: With great excitement or eagerness.
examples: Fans waited *breathlessly* for the announcement.
The press reported *breathlessly* on every detail of the wedding.

senses.gloss: In a cheerful, relaxed, casual way.
examples: "Don't worry about it," she said *breezily*.
He *breezily* dismissed the criticism.
The book is *breezily* written and easy to read.

form: flat — the same form as the adjective *bright*
contrast: Only after *shine* and *burn*, and in *bright and early*. Elsewhere use *brightly*: *she smiled brightly*.

senses.gloss: With a lot of light.
examples: The stars were shining *bright* over the desert.
The fire burned *brighter* as the wind picked up.
We have to be up *bright* and early tomorrow.

position: end — also before a past participle: *brightly lit*

senses.gloss: With a lot of light or strong color.
examples: The sun was shining *brightly*.
The room was *brightly* painted in yellow and blue.
The store windows were *brightly* lit.

senses.gloss: In a cheerful, lively way.
examples: "Good morning!" she said *brightly*.
He smiled *brightly* at the new neighbors.

senses.gloss: Extremely well; with great skill.
examples: She played the role *brilliantly*.
The plan worked *brilliantly*.
He *brilliantly* solved the problem in minutes.

senses.gloss: With very bright light or color.
examples: The stars shone *brilliantly* in the desert sky.
The trees were full of *brilliantly* colored birds.

senses.gloss: In a quick, energetic way.
examples: We walked *briskly* to stay warm.
Tickets sold *briskly* after the announcement.
"Let's get started," she said *briskly*.

position: front — *broadly speaking*; also mid or end

senses.gloss: In general, without the details.
examples: *Broadly* speaking, the plan was a success.
I *broadly* agree with what you're saying.
The two studies reached *broadly* similar conclusions.

senses.gloss: Widely and openly, of a smile.
examples: He grinned *broadly* when he saw us.
She was smiling *broadly* as she accepted the award.

modifies: verbs of hitting and turning, mainly *hit* and *strike*
contrast: More often a noun: *launch a broadside against the mayor* means to attack him in strong words. For cars, everyday American speech also says *T-boned*.

senses.gloss: With the whole side facing or hit by something.
examples: A truck ran the red light and hit our car *broadside*.
The boat was struck *broadside* by a huge wave.
The ship swung *broadside* to the wind.

senses.gloss: In a short, rude, abrupt way.
examples: "Not now," he said *brusquely*.
The nurse *brusquely* told us to wait outside.
She answered *brusquely* and hung up.

position: end — before its word as a degree word: *brutally honest*

senses.gloss: In a very cruel or violent way.
examples: The prisoners were *brutally* beaten.
The protest was *brutally* put down by the army.

senses.gloss: Extremely, of something harsh or unpleasant.
examples: To be *brutally* honest, I didn't like the movie.
It was a *brutally* hot summer in Phoenix.
The schedule was *brutally* demanding.

senses.gloss: In an active way, with a lot to do.
examples: The staff were *busily* preparing for the holidays.
She was typing *busily* when I walked in.
Bees buzzed *busily* around the flowers.

type: focusing — formal; also degree in *all but*
contrast: Normally a conjunction (*small but strong*). As an adverb meaning *only* it is formal or literary. *All but* before an adjective or verb means *almost* (*all but impossible*), but before a noun it means *everyone or everything except* (*all but one*).

senses.gloss: Only; no more than.
examples: She was *but* a child when the war began.
This is *but* one example of the problem.
Life is *but* a dream.

senses.gloss: Almost, in the phrase *all but*.
examples: By noon the snow had *all but* disappeared.
Finishing on time is now *all but* impossible.

senses.gloss: In a careful, secretive way that avoids giving information.
examples: He answered *cagily* when asked about his plans.
The senator spoke *cagily* about a run for president.
She smiled *cagily* and changed the subject.

senses.gloss: In a cruel way that shows no concern for others' feelings.
examples: The company *callously* fired workers by text message.
He *callously* ignored her pleas for help.
The refugees were treated *callously* at the border.

senses.gloss: In a quiet, relaxed way, without getting upset.
examples: She *calmly* explained what had happened.
Please walk *calmly* to the nearest exit.
He took the bad news *calmly*.

position: end — also front, as a comment

senses.gloss: In an honest, open way.
examples: She spoke *candidly* about her divorce.
*Candidly*, I don't think the plan will work.
He *candidly* admitted he had made a mistake.

senses.gloss: In a clever, shrewd way, especially about money or business.
examples: She *cannily* bought the property before prices rose.
The campaign *cannily* targeted young voters.
He had *cannily* saved for years.

senses.gloss: With skill and competence.
examples: She handled the crisis *capably*.
The deputy ran the office *capably* while the boss was away.
The team *capably* managed a very difficult project.

senses.gloss: In a sudden, unpredictable way, without a good reason.
examples: The rules seemed to be applied *capriciously*.
The weather changes *capriciously* in the mountains.
The manager fired people *capriciously*.

senses.gloss: With caution, so as to avoid harm or damage.
examples: Drive *carefully* — the roads are icy.
She *carefully* lifted the baby out of the car seat.

senses.gloss: With close attention to detail; thoroughly.
examples: Please read the instructions *carefully*.
The speech had been *carefully* planned.
Listen *carefully* to what I'm about to say.

senses.gloss: Without enough care or attention.
examples: He *carelessly* left the front door unlocked.
Someone had *carelessly* tossed a cigarette into the dry grass.
Her coat was thrown *carelessly* over a chair.

position: after its word — after the year or century
contrast: *C.E.* goes after the year (*79 C.E.*), while the older *A.D.* traditionally goes before it (*A.D. 79*).

senses.gloss: In the Common Era; the same years as *A.D.*, used after a year.
examples: Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 *C.E.*
The city was founded around 300 *C.E.*
By the fifth century *C.E.*, the empire had split in two.
